content: The national prevalence of early warning indicators (EWIs) can be estimated by combining data from randomly sampled clinics and conveniently sampled clinics. This approach involves abstracting data from antiretroviral therapy (ART) clinics and assessing data quality. The method allows for the expansion of EWI reporting through random sampling of ART clinics within a country, enabling a progressive scale-up of reporting to all clinics over time in a representative manner. Primary sampling refers to the selection of clinics, while secondary sampling involves selecting patients within those clinics. Ideally, EWIs should be reported annually from all ART clinics in a country. However, in cases where this is not feasible, a multi-year scale-up approach is recommended. For example, a country may begin by sampling 20% of clinics in the first year, then expand coverage by an additional 20% each year until all clinics are reporting by the fifth year. Clinics can be selected using a combination of random and convenience sampling, with results summarized in a nationally representative manner through weighting. Clinics with historical EWI reporting or readily available data, such as those with electronic medical records (EMRs), should continue to be included due to the lower cost of data abstraction. Secondary sampling involves collecting patient-level data within clinics for all EWIs except drug stock-outs. Whenever possible, data should be abstracted for all eligible patients (a census). The sample size required for secondary sampling depends on the size of the eligible patient population for each EWI. For example, the eligible population for on-time ARV drug pick-up (pediatric) includes all pediatric patients in care or receiving ART at the clinic during the reporting period. For retention on ART (adult), the eligible population includes adult patients who initiated ART during a specific reporting period and remained in care after 12 months. Sample size calculations are designed to achieve 95% confidence intervals with a margin of error of ±7%. After data abstraction, each clinic calculates the EWIs and assigns classifications (red, amber, green, or grey) based on thresholds. A grey classification is used when ≥30% of data is missing. It is not necessary to calculate confidence intervals to assign classifications. At the national level, countries should report the proportion of clinics achieving each classification for each indicator and patient population (adult and pediatric). This allows program managers to identify areas needing improvement and monitor progress over time. Results can be presented in a scorecard format, which is easily interpretable by stakeholders and ministries of health. Nationally representative prevalence estimates for each EWI can be calculated by aggregating and weighting data from sampled clinics. Clinics with larger patient populations are weighted more heavily than smaller clinics. Aggregation should only be performed if ≥70% of data is available for the nationally eligible population monitored by a specific indicator. If less than 70% of data is available, aggregation should not be performed. These assessments help identify systemic issues in record-keeping and inform changes to improve patient monitoring systems and clinic practices. Data abstraction can be performed using paper-based or electronic medical records. If paper-based records are used, trained clinic staff should abstract data retrospectively, typically once per year. When electronic medical records are available, data abstraction should be guided by national program experts. Clinics with >30% missing data for a specific indicator should be classified as grey, signaling the need for support in record-keeping. In summary, the systematic monitoring of EWIs through representative sampling, data abstraction, and quality assessments provides critical insights into ART program performance at both clinic and national levels. This process supports evidence-based decision-making and programmatic improvements to enhance the quality of HIV care and treatment.
